title: Siegel-zero scenario check: what if L(1,χ_{−4p}) is tiny?
connection: k₂ and R correlate positively with L(1,χ_{−4p}); an exceptional (Siegel) discriminant −4p would make Type II/(★) starve; Type I is χ_p-driven and unaffected.
why: Suggests ES is robust to Siegel zeros via Type I (complementarity), aligning with the campaign's 'Siegel dichotomy' discussion.

title: Kloosterman sums K(1,1;p) vs ES counts (null test)
connection: Normalised Kloosterman sums are Sato–Tate distributed; correlate with residual U(p) at p ≤ 2·10⁴.
why: Kloosterman sums appear in the spectral treatment of divisor problems in progressions (the X(n) part); a correlation at the pointwise level would be surprising.

title: 105 = 3·5·7 vs 385 = 5·7·11: products of consecutive odd primes in exceptional sets
connection: 105 is a zero of all our word families; 385 is in A396825 but our families certify it; 33 = 3·11 likewise.
why: Squarefree products of small odd primes are 'locally saturated' (n ≡ 0 mod many small q kills many shifts); a cheap structural family to test any certificate system on: 15015, 255255, …
first_step: Compute R, Uv, I3, ESC at products of consecutive odd primes up to 3·10⁶ (105, 1155, 15015, 255255) and at 3·5·7·m² forms.

title: Σ_{p ≤ N} f(p) / (N log² N) = 0.88, 0.80, 0.77, 0.76, 0.75 (N = 10³…2·10⁵)
connection: ET prove N log²N ≪ Σ_{p≤N} f(p) ≪ N log²N log log N; our ordered counts give a slowly decreasing ratio to N log²N (and 0.45 → 0.30 against N log²N loglog N) — the data favour the lower-bound order, with a constant ≈ 0.7.
why: Suggests (does not pin down) that the log log factor in ET's upper bound may be absent — relevant to which heuristic mean (BM, Euler product) is calibrated correctly.
first_step: Extend to 10⁷ via windows; fit c + d/log N.

title: Σ_{n ≤ N} f(n) grows faster than N log³N in range (ratio 7.6 → 19.6 for N = 10³ → 3·10⁴)
connection: Over all n (composites included) the ordered-count partial sums outgrow N log³N; composite n with many divisors carry large counts.
why: Composite counts are dominated by divisor-rich n; irrelevant to ES existence but important if one uses averages over all n as a proxy for primes (wrong normalisation by a log² factor).
first_step: Check ET's statement for Σ_{n≤N} f(n) (if any) and fit the exponent of log.

title: U(p) and the least prime ≡ 1 (mod p) or the least prime q with p | q − 1 (Linnik-type)
connection: Null-expected cross check: data about primes in progressions modulo p (EXSET_LINNIK.md) should not influence local ES counts.
why: Sanity: separates 'divisor-in-progression' events used in ES (which are about divisors of p-tied integers) from progressions mod p.
first_step: Compute least prime q ≡ 1 (mod p) for p ≤ 2·10⁴ and Spearman with residual U.

title: Divisor switching with a moving modulus
connection: Exchange the roles of a target divisor and its complementary factor in the p-tied divisor count.
why: The same certificate can be counted in two ranges, potentially exposing different analytic structure.
first_step: Write both exact summation orders for divisors d≡−1 modulo 4C of 4Cp+1.

title: Exceptional-prime clustering
connection: Study whether primes with few bounded certificates cluster in arithmetic progressions or short intervals.
why: Structure in the tail could suggest targeted constructions rather than more uniform averaging.
first_step: Define one fixed search budget and compare the bottom count decile across residue classes and intervals.

title: Smooth auxiliary values
connection: Favor parameters for which the p-tied integer has many small prime factors, then inspect whether their divisor residues cover the target.
why: Smoothness supplies many selectable factors but does not by itself settle residue coverage.
first_step: Search C≤100 for primes below 1000 and correlate smoothness with target-residue success.

title: Rough–smooth complementary constructions
connection: Pair a construction exploiting many small factors with one exploiting a single large complementary factor.
why: The two regimes may produce genuinely different certificate mechanisms.
first_step: Partition auxiliary values by largest-prime-factor ratio and compare the successful denominator shapes.

title: Chebotarev questions for family selection
connection: Ask whether a family-selection condition is a Frobenius condition in a fixed finite extension.
why: If it is, an existing distribution theorem might describe which primes select that family, not automatically all primes.
first_step: For one proposed selector, build the extension and check whether its predicate really depends only on Frobenius.

title: Pretentious character diagnostics
connection: Compare stubborn divisor-residue biases with multiplicative functions that mimic simple characters on small primes.
why: A structured bias could suggest a complementary family tailored to that character.
first_step: Compute distances between empirical factor-sign patterns and a small library of Dirichlet characters.

title: Bohr-set parameter windows
connection: Interpret simultaneous near-integral rational expressions in a parametrization as a finite Bohr-set-like condition.
why: Approximate alignment can identify intervals where exact divisibility is worth testing.
first_step: For two explicit rational coefficient conditions, plot simultaneous fractional-part windows over the parameter range.

title: Discrepancy of admissible parameters
connection: Measure deviation of successful parameter residues from uniformity across intervals.
why: A useful discrepancy bound could turn a dense parameter set into an explicit interval witness.
first_step: For a fixed family, compute interval discrepancy at several cutoffs and distinguish local biases from global drift.

title: Sieve parity diagnostics
connection: Check which certificate predicates depend only on roughness and which depend on the parity or residue of factor products.
why: This identifies information a chosen sieve model must retain, without discarding the connection.
first_step: Construct two auxiliary integers with matching small-prime divisibility data but different target-divisor behavior.

title: Vector-valued sieving
connection: Keep several certificate-family weights simultaneously rather than collapsing them into one scalar sieve weight.
why: Different families may respond differently to the same local exclusion.
first_step: Tabulate a vector of local survival indicators for three families modulo the first five primes.

title: Dense-model questions for divisor residues
connection: Ask whether a normalized divisor-residue measure resembles a simpler measure on the test functions relevant to ES.
why: Only the relevant tests need approximation, so a tailored model might be more useful than global uniformity.
first_step: Specify a finite test-function family and solve for a simple measure matching its moments.

title: Toda-like recurrences of continuants
connection: Compare determinant recurrences of tridiagonal matrices with short continued-fraction certificate expressions.
why: Shared determinant algebra may suggest bilinear recurrence identities useful for composition.
first_step: Compute adjacent tridiagonal minors symbolically and test their identities against a short continuant parametrization.

title: Arcsine law for divisors applied to 4Cp+1
connection: Deshouillers–Dress–Tenenbaum: divisors of a typical n are arcsine-distributed on the log scale ↔ ES needs a divisor of 4Cp+1 in a specific residue class −1 mod 4C, for SOME C.
why: Averaging over C (not over p) is a legitimate thick object at a fixed p; the arcsine law tells where divisors cluster, suggesting which C-range to aim at.
first_step: Search 'arcsine law divisors residue class' and check whether a residue-class-restricted DDT theorem exists (Tenenbaum's work on divisors in APs); then test numerically on 4Cp+1, C ≤ p, for fixed p.
alt_first_steps: [tools-0033] Compute the joint distribution of (log d/log N, d mod 4C) for N = 4Cp+1 and check independence numerically.
refs: Deshouillers, Dress, Tenenbaum, Lois de répartition des diviseurs (1979)
Deshouillers–Dress–Tenenbaum, Lois de répartition des diviseurs, Acta Arith. 34 (1979)

title: Schwinger–Dyson / loop equations for the generating function of f(n)
connection: Define F(s) = Σ f(n) n^{−s}. Elsholtz–Tao estimate partial sums; a functional equation or 'loop equation' for F (from the multiplicative structure of the Type I/II divisor conditions) might give analytic continuation and thus pointwise info via a Perron formula with explicit kernels.
why: Repo has anal_dirichlet_series.md; the free-lane twist is to look for an algebraic relation among F and its twists rather than estimates.
first_step: git grep -il 'dirichlet series' BRAINSTORM; then compute F(s) numerically for Re s > 1 and test whether F(s)/ζ(s)³ or F(s)/ζ(s)²L(s,χ₋₄) is 'nice' (bounded, Euler product).
refs: BRAINSTORM/anal_dirichlet_series.md

title: Hydrodynamic limit of Elsholtz–Tao's f(n) along short intervals
connection: Σ_{n∈[N,N+H]} f(n) for H = N^θ: short-interval averages (Matomäki–Radziwiłł technology) of multiplicative-like functions. f is not multiplicative, but its Type I count is a divisor-type sum.
why: Short-interval results for divisor-type functions are strong (every short interval of length N^{0.5+ε} has its expected count); pushing H down to log^A N along primes would be 'almost pointwise'.
first_step: Search 'divisor function short intervals every interval' (Ivić, Matomäki); check what H is attainable for d(n) restricted to residue classes and whether the Type I count fits.
refs: Matomäki–Radziwiłł, Multiplicative functions in short intervals

title: Constraint-propagation / arc-consistency on the (c,d,f) space to prove 'no solution' is contradictory
connection: CSP solvers find contradictions by propagating constraints; for a *symbolic* p (represented by its residues mod many small moduli), propagation might derive that 'no solution for any C ≤ K' contradicts p being prime ≡ 1 mod 24 for some K.
why: This is the covering-system search re-done with a general-purpose propagator that can also use quadratic-residuosity constraints (not just congruences) — which Mordell–Schinzel does not forbid.
first_step: Compute, for each q ≤ 200, the allowed residues of p mod q given all certificates with modulus q; multiply densities.
alt_first_steps: [free_fable-0079] Encode: p ≡ r mod 840; for each C ≤ K, all divisors of 4Cp+1 ≡ −1 mod 4C forbidden ⟹ constraints on Legendre symbols (−C/q) for q | 4Cp+1; propagate; look for contradiction with K ≤ 20.
refs: Mordell–Schinzel

title: Probabilistic method with alterations on the (c,d) grid: a second-moment bound for the tied-modulus count for an *explicit* subfamily of p
connection: Second-moment (Chebyshev) + alterations proves existence for almost all p; the question is whether for *structured* p (e.g. p = 1 + 24m with m having all small primes as factors) the variance is small enough to prove f(p) ≥ 1 unconditionally.
why: 'Almost all' results can sometimes be upgraded to 'all p in an explicit sparse set', which would be a new infinite case of ES (the campaign says no infinite case is proved! Though Mordell identities cover residue classes… those are infinite sets of n but not of primes? Mordell's identities DO cover infinitely many primes; what is open is only square classes). So the target: an explicit infinite set of primes inside the square classes mod 840.
first_step: Check FRONTIER §5 for what is known about explicit infinite subsets of hard primes; then try: primes p with p ≡ 1 mod 840 and 4p+1 ≡ 0 mod 5 … construct a sub-family where a fixed C wins by a *non-polynomial* reason (e.g. p such that 4p + 1 is 5 × a prime ≡ −1 mod 4? that's a prime-value condition, not a residue class — and indeed gives infinitely many p conditionally on Dickson).
refs: FRONTIER.md §5

title: Linnik's theorem and its 'one prime in an AP' nature as the template for 'one divisor in a class'
connection: Linnik: the least prime in an AP mod q is ≤ q^L. It's a pointwise (for every q) statement with polylog... no, with a *power* of q reservoir. ES's reservoir is the divisors of ONE number — but over C there are infinitely many numbers 4Cp+1. Reframe: is there a 'Linnik for shifted multiples': for every p, some C ≤ p^A has 4Cp+1 with a prime factor ≡ −1 mod 4C?
why: With C up to p^A the reservoir IS power-sized, so Linnik-type methods (zero-density, log-free) might apply — this is a *different* (weaker-looking but still ES-implying) target the repo's B3 critique may not cover, since the certificate count over C ≤ p^A is ≫ p^{A−o(1)}... wait, does C ≤ p^A keep the count polylog? The expected number of winning C ≤ X is ≈ Σ_{C≤X} 1/φ(4C)·(something) ≈ log X·const — still only log. Hmm: that's the campaign's point (B3). But Linnik's problem ALSO has only ~q^L/φ(q)·(1/log) expected primes... no, it has many. Record the count honestly and still try: the *prime-divisor* certificate count over C ≤ p^A.
first_step: Search for literature on 'prime factors in residue classes of a fixed integer' (e.g. 'prime divisors of shifted primes in arithmetic progressions', Moree).
alt_first_steps: [free_fable-0131] Compute E[#{C ≤ X: 4Cp+1 has a prime factor ≡ −1 mod 4C}] empirically for p ≈ 10⁶ and X up to 10⁶; fit log X vs power growth.
refs: Linnik's theorem

title: Ramanujan's 'highly composite' intuition: do primes p for which 4Cp+1 is highly composite for some small C always have solutions trivially? (converse direction for hard primes)
connection: Hard primes should be those for which 4Cp+1 has few prime factors for all small C — i.e. p such that 4Cp+1 is prime or nearly prime for C = 1..K. 'Prime-producing' primes p (4p+1, 8p+1, 12p+1 all prime) are rare (Hardy–Littlewood) but infinitely many conjecturally; are those the only hard ones?
why: If hardness ⟺ 'all 4Cp+1 are nearly prime' then ES failure needs a 'prime constellation' of unbounded length — impossible by sieve upper bounds! (Any fixed length is fine, but failing at ALL C ≤ K with K → ∞ needs 4Cp+1 ∈ {prime or product of primes ≡ 1 mod 4C...}.) Check whether the 'all nearly prime' heuristic for failure matches data.
first_step: For p ≤ 10⁷, correlate C_min(p) with Σ_{C ≤ 10} ω(4Cp+1); check whether large C_min ⟺ small ω's.
refs: Hardy–Littlewood prime k-tuples

title: Representation theory: the count of divisors in class −1 mod 4C is a trace of a permutation representation
connection: #{d | N : d ≡ r mod m} = (1/φ(m)) Σ_χ χ̄(r) Σ_{d|N} χ(d); the inner sum is a 'twisted divisor function' σ₀(N, χ) which is the Fourier coefficient of an Eisenstein series E(χ, χ̄). Summing over C (with N = 4Cp+1, m = 4C) is summing coefficients of a *varying-level* Eisenstein family at the arguments 4Cp+1 — a 'horizontal' sum across levels.
why: Varying-level sums of Eisenstein coefficients have appeared in the theory of 'moments of L-functions over a family of levels' (e.g. Conrey–Iwaniec); positivity results for such family sums exist on average over the argument but here the argument is tied to the level.
first_step: Write Σ_{C≤X} σ₀(4Cp+1; χ_C-component) explicitly; look for a Petersson/Kuznetsov-type formula that handles 'argument = 4Cp+1 tied to level 4C'; search 'Eisenstein series coefficients at n ≡ 1 mod level'.
refs: Conrey–Iwaniec 2000

title: Shifted divisor problem at fixed shift p: Σ_{C ≤ X} τ(4Cp+1) with X ≪ p^ε — the 'short range' regime
connection: Classical: Σ_{n ≤ X} τ(an + b) ~ (main) for X ≫ a^{1+ε} or so; ES needs C only up to polylog(p) ideally (so X ≪ a^ε, far below the classical range). In the short range, the sum is dominated by the structure of the specific p — i.e. exactly the pointwise regime. Known results: for X ≥ a^{1/2+ε}? (Friedlander–Iwaniec, divisor function in APs to large moduli; Fouvry). For X < a^{1/2} essentially nothing is known pointwise.
why: Pins down the exact analytic barrier: ES(p) with C ≤ p^θ requires understanding τ(4Cp+1)-type sums with C ≤ p^θ; θ < 1/2 is beyond current technology for the *unrestricted* divisor sum, let alone the class-restricted one. But θ ≥ 1 (C up to p) IS within technology for the unrestricted sum — so 'ES with C ≤ p' might be attackable via large-modulus divisor results if the class restriction can be handled by characters (log-many characters…).
first_step: Read Fouvry–Iwaniec / Friedlander–Iwaniec on τ in APs to moduli q ≤ x^{2/3}; map to Σ_{C ≤ X} τ(4Cp + 1) with p as the 'modulus' and X as the range: need X ≥ p^{3/2}? Record the exact requirement.
refs: Friedlander–Iwaniec, 'Incomplete Kloosterman sums and a divisor problem' (Ann. Math 1985)
Fouvry 1985

title: Weighted counts: instead of counting certificates, weight each by a function w(C, a) chosen to make the sum provably positive
connection: Counting with weights w ≥ 0 that vanish on 'hard' regions can make the error term smaller relative to the main term; Selberg-sieve weights (λ_d) are the classical example, and Maynard's multi-dimensional weights broke the bounded-gaps problem. For ES: weight certificates by smoothness of a, by C^{−s}, by Legendre-symbol filters.
why: Weight optimisation is a standard move that changed outcomes in sieve theory; the ES count has never (?) been weighted beyond C^{−s}.
first_step: Define a parametrised weight family (e.g. w = Λ-type weights on C or on a) and numerically compute the ratio (weighted count)/(its p-average) for p ≤ 10⁶; find weights minimising the spread of the ratio (i.e. maximising concentration), then analyse the best one.
refs: Maynard, 'Small gaps between primes'

title: Count of representations with multiplicity: Σ_{solutions} 1 vs Σ_{solutions} 1/(stabiliser) — Siegel-mass-style weighted counts might be more 'modular'
connection: Siegel's mass formula is exact for weighted counts (by 1/|Aut|); for ES, 'automorphisms' are permutations of equal coordinates; weighting by 1/|Stab| makes f(n) a 'mass'. If the mass has an exact formula (e.g. a divisor-sum identity) for some sub-count, that's rigid structure.
why: Checking whether any ES sub-count satisfies an exact identity (like r₂(n) = 4Σ χ₄(d)) is cheap and would be a major structural discovery.
first_step: Compute the Type II mass m_II(n) = Σ 1/|Stab| for n ≤ 10⁴; test multiplicativity, test against OEIS, test linear relations with τ(n), σ(n), r₂(n), h(−4n).
refs: Siegel mass formula

title: Composite exceptions to the C-form: which non-square n < 10⁵ have no 4Cn+1 = ab, a ≡ b ≡ −1 (4C)?
connection: The C-form does not use primality, so it's a statement about all n. Odd squares fail (T1). Which other n fail? Among primes 409, 577, 5569, 9601 (C < 1500). Composite failures would show whether the C-form exceptional set is 'squares + sporadic' or has infinite non-square families.
why: Cheap census that characterises a natural sub-conjecture; the structure of composite exceptions (do they factor as square × something? products of C-form exceptions?) is informative.
first_step: Compute for all n ≤ 10⁵ (n ≡ 1 mod 4; also check n ≡ 3 mod 4 which has a different parity structure) whether a C-form certificate exists with C ≤ 2000; list non-square failures; factor them.
refs: scripts/z52b_free_fable_sanity.py

title: Quadratic divisor problem (DFI): Σ τ(n) τ(n + h) and Σ τ(an + b)… the ES count as a 'twisted divisor sum along a quadratic sequence'
connection: Type I: Σ_c #{f | p² + 4c²d, f ≡ −p (4cd)} is a divisor sum along the quadratic polynomial 4dc² + p² in c, with a residue condition tied to c. Divisor sums along quadratic polynomials (Hooley's Σ τ(n² + 1), and the general theory for Σ τ(f(n)) by Hooley, Bykovskii, and recent work by Browning / Sofos) have asymptotics with power savings — *for the unrestricted sum*.
why: The unrestricted Σ_{c ≤ X} τ(p² + 4c²d) has a known asymptotic (Hooley-type) with explicit dependence on the polynomial's discriminant (−16dp²... depends on p!). Pointwise-in-p control of the error is exactly the uniformity question; the literature's dependence on the coefficients is explicit enough to check.
first_step: Read Hooley 'On the number of divisors of quadratic polynomials' (Acta Math 1963) and extract the uniformity in the polynomial's coefficients; apply to p² + 4dc² with X ≈ p^θ.
alt_first_steps: [signature-0027] Search: 'divisors of n² + a in arithmetic progressions uniformly in a'; compute the Type I count vs. Hooley-type prediction at fixed p.
refs: Hooley, Acta Math. 110 (1963)
Bykovskii 1984
unverified: Hooley 1963, On the number of divisors of a quadratic polynomial (Acta Math.)

title: Sieve of Eratosthenes generalisation: 'sieve by certificates' — remove from [1, X] all n certified by (C, a) with a ≤ A; what remains?
connection: The uncovered integers after sieving by all C-form classes with a ≤ A form a 'sifted set'; its density and the structure of its elements as A grows are exactly computable; compare with the sieve-theoretic prediction Π (1 − 1/a) — the discrepancy measures the correlation structure (classes are not independent).
why: A direct empirical measure of the 'independence' heuristic, which underlies the exp(−log²p) prediction; strong positive correlation would mean failures cluster (good for proofs: fewer independent events to control).
first_step: Compute the sifted set for X = 10⁶ and A up to 10⁴; compare its size with the independence prediction; inspect the residue structure of survivors.

title: Gallagher's larger sieve for the ES exceptional set: exploit that exceptions avoid MANY classes mod each a
connection: Gallagher's larger sieve is efficient when the sifted set avoids most classes mod each prime (ω(q) close to q); ES exceptions avoid only one class per (C, a) — so Gallagher is wrong tool; but for the full Type II family, a given a is a modulus for many (c,d) (all with 4cd | a + 1) with DIFFERENT classes r_{c,d,a} = −(4c²d)^{−1} mod a, so the number of avoided classes mod a is #{(c,d): 4cd | a+1} ≈ τ-many distinct classes (are they distinct? −(4c²d)^{-1} for different (c,d) with the same cd... c²d = c·(cd), so different c with the same cd give different classes). Still ≪ a, so the larger sieve doesn't bite. Record as negative.
why: Closes a door cheaply, and the count of 'distinct avoided classes per modulus a' is itself the key quantity for any sieve bound — tabulate it.
first_step: For a ≤ 10⁴, compute ω(a) = #{distinct classes −(4c²d)^{-1} mod a over (c,d) with 4cd | a+1}; its average order vs a.
refs: Gallagher, 'A larger sieve' (1971)

title: Tied equidistribution: factors of (p + 2c√−d) in ray class groups of conductor 4cd as c varies — a 'horizontal Chebotarev' with growing conductor
connection: Standard Chebotarev: fixed field, varying prime. Here: fixed prime p, varying field/conductor (4cd), and the element p + 2c√−d varies with c. Is there any theorem on equidistribution of Frobenius-like data in a tower of ray class fields at a FIXED prime? (Reminiscent of 'p splits completely in K_n for infinitely many n' questions, Iwasawa theory, and of Kummer-type 'order of p mod n' statistics: p's residue mod n as n varies is equidistributed trivially; but the ideal factorisation of p + 2c√−d mod 4c is like 'p's behaviour in the ray class field', not controlled by p alone.)
why: Naming the exact missing theorem ('horizontal Chebotarev at a fixed prime') makes it searchable and askable (MO/people items).
first_step: Search 'equidistribution ray class group fixed prime varying conductor' and 'Chebotarev tower fixed prime'; ask on MO if nothing.

title: GRH-conditional ES via effective Chebotarev in Kummer-type families: what does the campaign already know?
connection: FRONTIER §5 lists conditional results (GRH, Dickson, Hypothesis H, SEL). Check whether 'ES on GRH' is known to fail for a specific reason (e.g. the conductors grow too fast: effective Chebotarev gives a prime of norm ≤ (log D)² where D ≈ (4cd)^{something}; a certificate needs an ideal of norm f ≤ p² + 4c²d dividing a SPECIFIC element — not a free prime — so Chebotarev doesn't apply directly).
why: Prevents duplicating a known dead end; the 'specific element' obstruction is B2 in Chebotarev clothing — record it, but check whether Hooley's trick (sieve over k with GRH) circumvents the 'specific element' issue since Artin's conjecture also concerns a specific element a.
first_step: Read FRONTIER §5 conditional entries; write a half-page comparing Artin (specific a, free q) vs ES (specific p, free (c,d), but the divisor must divide a specific number) and identify precisely where the Artin method's 'free q' is used.
refs: FRONTIER.md §5

title: Joint failure for C = 1 and C = 2: p with 4p+1 all factors ≡ 1 mod 4 AND 8p+1 failing the mod-8 pattern — a two-condition sieve whose density and *correlation* are computable
connection: The two conditions concern 4p+1 and 8p+1, linear forms in p with gcd(4p+1, 8p+1) | 1... (8p+1 − 2(4p+1) = −1, so coprime). Independence of the two factorisations is the sieve heuristic; the actual joint density vs the product of marginals quantifies the correlation (via p's residues mod small primes which affect both).
why: If the joint failure density factorises (independence holds to good accuracy), the heuristic exp(−Σ) stands; the correlation structure at small C is where any 'conspiracy' enabling a counterexample would show up.
first_step: Compute the joint and marginal failure frequencies for C ∈ {1,2,3,4,6} over p ≤ 10⁷; compute all pairwise correlations.

title: Which composites fail the C-form? Test whether C-form exceptions are closed under multiplication by squares or by other exceptions
connection: If n fails the C-form, does n·m² fail? (T1-like scaling: for squares the obstruction is via (a/m²) = 1; for n·m²: (a/nm²) = (a/n) — so the QNR condition reduces to that of n; and 4C·nm² + 1 = ab with a ≡ −1 (4C) — different integer.) Empirically test closure properties of the exceptional set E = {n : no C-form certificate}.
why: Structural properties of E (closure, multiplicativity) constrain any eventual characterisation; e.g. if E ⊇ {odd squares} ∪ {409 m² : m odd}, there are infinite non-square families, changing the 'squares + sporadic' expectation for this sub-conjecture.

title: Analogy: 'primes p such that p + 1 is a sum of two squares' (Iwaniec) — the half-dimensional sieve as the exact tool for 'C = 1 fails'
connection: C = 1 fails ⟺ 4p+1 has all prime factors ≡ 1 mod 4 ⟺ 4p+1 is 'primitively' a sum of two squares with no factor ≡ 3 mod 4 — the half-dimensional sieve's territory (Iwaniec 1972: #{p ≤ x: p + 1 = a² + b²} ≍ x/(log x)^{3/2}). So #{p ≤ x: C=1 fails} ≍ x/(log x)^{3/2}: a THEOREM-level statement (upper AND lower bounds) about the simplest failure set.
why: Gives the first rigorous 'failure-set size' at C = 1 with matching lower bound — a template for C ≤ K failure sets and a sanity anchor for all heuristics (the constant can be compared with data).
first_step: Check Iwaniec's theorem applies to 4p+1 (linear form in p with leading coefficient 4; yes, 'Primes of the type φ(x,y) + A'/'half-dimensional sieve' handle p + A; for 4p + 1 check the admissibility); compute the constant and compare with the empirical count up to 10⁷.
refs: Iwaniec, 'Primes of the type φ(x,y)+A where φ is a quadratic form', Acta Arith 21 (1972)

title: Upper-bound sieve on simultaneous failure for C ∈ {1, 2}: #{p ≤ x : 4p+1 ∈ S₁ and 8p+1 ∈ S₂} ≪ x/(log x)^{1+1/2+δ₂}
connection: Each extra C with an index-2-type failure set adds 1/2 to the sieve dimension; S₂ (mod 8 patterns) has 'dimension' depending on which residue classes mod 8 are excluded from the subset-product condition (computed via the failure patterns). A K-fold simultaneous Landau sieve with dimension κ_K = Σ_C δ_C and explicit constants.
why: For fixed K this is a theorem-level upper bound; the K → ∞ uniformity gives exceptional-set bounds; and comparing with data at K = 2, 3 is a precise calibration of sieve constants vs reality.
first_step: Compute δ_C (the density exponent of S_C) for C ≤ 6 from the failure patterns; run a Selberg sieve numerically for K = 2 to get the constant; compare with the empirical joint-failure count to 10⁷.

title: Vaughan's proof as a fixed point: re-derive with modern large-sieve inequalities
connection: Vaughan 1970 used the large sieve ↔ modern variants (Iwaniec's bilinear, multiplicative large sieve for sparse moduli, Baier–Zhao for square moduli).
why: Campaign has 3/4 exponent; large sieve for moduli of special form (e.g. 4uB) may give a different exponent shape.
first_step: Check whether a large sieve for moduli in the multiplicative semigroup {4uB} (product moduli) exists in literature (search 'large sieve product moduli').

title: Two-stage ES tree with Huang–Vaughan binary statistics at the second stage
connection: Generic form: write 4/p as a sum of two fractions each with numerator 1 or 2 in a specific way ↔ ES via 4/p = 1/x + 3/(px')…
why: Splits ES into a two-step tree; each step is binary Egyptian (well-understood: Huang–Vaughan counts).
first_step: Enumerate decompositions 4/p = 1/x + r/s with r/s a 2-term-representable fraction and compare count distribution with Huang–Vaughan binary statistics.

title: Weight-1 forms and Kronecker characters: M_BM as a sum of class numbers
connection: M_BM(p) = Σ (1 − χ_{−4uB}(p))/φ(4uB) is an average of characters ↔ L(1,χ) and class numbers of ℚ(√−uB·p)?
why: Swapping sum order may give M_BM(p) as a weighted sum of L-values attached to p; class-number lower bounds (Siegel, Goldfeld) are pointwise.
first_step: Rewrite T(p) = Σ (−uB/p)/φ(4uB) by grouping by m = uB: Σ_m (−m/p)·g(m) with g(m) = #{splittings}/φ(4m); compare with L(1, (−·/p))-weighted sums.

title: Rudnev point–plane incidences / Stevens–de Zeeuw in 𝔽_p for modular hyperbola data
connection: Rudnev's point-plane bound and Stevens–de Zeeuw point-line bounds over 𝔽_p give incidence counts beyond trivial; ES Type II solutions are points on modular hyperbolas ff′ ≡ 1 in boxes.
why: Incidence bounds control how many hyperbola points can concentrate, useful for second moments of R(p).
first_step: Count Type II certificate points as incidences between a point set {(f,f′)} and a family of hyperbolas indexed by (c,d) mod p; apply Stevens–de Zeeuw.
alt_first_steps: [free_opus-0082] Express ES(p) as existence of an incidence between a point set P_p and a line set L_p over F_p (or ℤ) and check sizes vs Rudnev's bound regime.

Rudnev, On the number of incidences between points and planes in three dimensions, Combinatorica 38 (2018)

title: Siegel's lemma with congruence conditions: a small solution of a linear system tied to p
connection: Siegel's lemma guarantees small integer solutions of underdetermined linear systems ↔ ES Type II linear in C for fixed (u,B).
why: For fixed u, the condition (4uC−1) | p+u is linear in a hidden quotient: p + u = k(4uC − 1); i.e. p = 4uCk − u − k: symmetric bilinear in (C,k)! Siegel can't force bilinear, but the structure is a 'multiplicative Siegel lemma'.
first_step: Note p + u + k = 4uCk: for fixed u, need p ≡ −u − k mod 4uk with C integer. Tabulate minimal u per p and the 'free' parameter k distribution.

title: Mixing of the map p ↦ (p mod 4uC−1) as u,C vary: equidistribution of residues of a single integer
connection: Residues of a fixed p modulo a growing family of moduli ↔ ES needs p ≡ −u mod (4uC−1) for some pair; this is 'one integer vs many moduli' — Erdős–Turán type discrepancy.
why: Discrepancy of {p/m} for m in a structured set is a classic (Vinogradov-type) problem; known results (e.g. on p mod m for m ≤ √p) might give existence in some ranges.
first_step: Measure discrepancy of fractional parts {(p+u)/(4uC−1)} over the trial set and compare with random; the ES event is the fractional part being exactly 0.

title: Billiards / circle rotation: p mod m for consecutive m as a rotation-like sequence
connection: p mod m for m near √p behaves like a quadratic sequence (Dirichlet divisor problem) ↔ ES divisibility events are zeros of p mod (4uC − 1).
why: Near m ≈ √p, p mod m follows parabolic arcs; divisors appear at structured places. Could the ES moduli family hit such arcs?
first_step: Plot (m, (p+u) mod m) for moduli m = 4uC−1 near √p and look for parabolic patterns permitting a forced zero.

title: Second moment method over primes in short intervals: positive proportion with R(p) ≥ 1 in every interval
connection: Paley–Zygmund on R over primes in [X, X+H] ↔ ES almost-all in short intervals.
why: Repo has interval results; second moment at H = (log X)^A would be a new 'every short interval contains many ES primes' result (weak but new form).
first_step: Check repo's (D)30 interval result range of H; compute what second moment would need for H = (log X)^A.

title: Littlewood conjecture analogy: inf n‖nα‖‖nβ‖ = 0 vs ES certificates as simultaneous small values
connection: Both ask for simultaneous small values of products of distances ↔ ES Type II p ≡ −(u+B) mod 4uB is a multiplicative Diophantine approximation condition.
why: Littlewood is open too, with measure-zero exceptional set (EKL) — a parallel of 'almost all' ES results; methods might transfer in either direction.
first_step: Write ES Type II as a product-of-distances condition and compare its structure with Littlewood's.

title: Index calculus analogy: smooth relations and linear algebra over (ℤ/4C)^×
connection: Index calculus finds discrete logs by collecting smooth relations ↔ ES gate: express −1 as a product of factor-base primes' classes, with the factor base = small primes dividing p-tied integers.
why: Linear algebra over exponent vectors mod the group exponent makes 'is −1 in the generated subgroup' decidable; collecting relations across many C might show the subgroup is always everything.
first_step: For hard p, collect smooth parts of 4Cp+1 for C ≤ 10³; for each C compute the subgroup generated mod 4C; record when it's proper.

title: Titchmarsh divisor problem with congruence: Σ_{p≤x} #{d | p+a : d ≡ r mod q}
connection: Summing ES certificate counts over p is a Titchmarsh-type divisor problem in progressions (Fouvry, Bombieri–Friedlander–Iwaniec). It controls averages and exceptional sets, as LORENZINI_W used Linnik/Halberstam.
why: This is the native average tool, already in the repo; recorded so the map is complete. BFI-level distribution beyond 1/2 could improve exceptional-set exponents.
first_step: Check whether BFI's level-4/7 results apply to the specific moduli 4C with the −1 class; if so, compute the resulting exceptional-set exponent.
alt_first_steps: [free_opus-0215] Check whether BFI-type level-of-distribution > 1/2 for fixed residue a applies to (4Cp+1) with class condition on divisors; estimate effect on 3/4 exponent.
[tools-0253] Write the Type II average as a Titchmarsh sum with residue restriction and check Drappeau–Topacogullari's uniformity in the residue modulus.
refs: Bombieri–Friedlander–Iwaniec 1986
LORENZINI_W.md §6
Drappeau–Topacogullari, Combinatorial identities and Titchmarsh's divisor problem for multiplicative functions, Algebra & Number Theory 13 (2019)

title: Selberg's Λ² upper-bound sieve inverted: lower bound for 'not all events fail' via Turán sieve
connection: Turán sieve gives lower bounds for counts of objects hitting at least one condition from variance ↔ R(p) pointwise needs variance over a p-family — no family at fixed p, but family over (u,C) trials.
why: Turán-type inequality at fixed p: #{success} ≥ (Σ P)²/(Σ_{i,j} P_ij) in a probabilistic model over trials; but the 'probability' at fixed p is deterministic. Identify a randomisation at fixed p (e.g. random auxiliary prime) that preserves certificates.
first_step: Search for an auxiliary random variable at fixed p (e.g. random multiplier λ with certificates for λp mapping back) — check if 4/p certificates can be transported from 4/(λp)-type statements.

title: Rational points of bounded height on the ES fibre counted by circle method in 3 variables? (Not enough variables) → use delta method on 4uBC − u − B = p
connection: Heath-Brown delta method counts representations by forms in ≥ 3 variables ↔ 4uBC − u − B = p is a cubic in 3 variables (degenerate: linear in each).
why: Multilinear forms are amenable to the circle method with fewer variables because of their structure (e.g. Kloosterman refinement for xy − zw); R(p) ~ main term log² p might be derivable but error bounds are the issue.
first_step: Set up delta-method counting of 4uBC − u − B = p with smooth weights; compute the singular series and integral; compare with M₀.

title: Divisor function in arithmetic progressions to large moduli (Fouvry–Iwaniec, Heath-Brown τ₃) applied to Σ_C
connection: τ in APs with modulus beyond √x (via Kloosterman, Deshouillers–Iwaniec) ↔ divisors of 4Cp+1 in class mod 4C averaged over C.
why: Average over C at fixed p is a genuine one-variable average (not over p) — exactly the kind of thick average available at a single p. Level-of-distribution results for τ(n) in APs n ≡ a mod q with q ~ n^{2/3} might count Σ_C at fixed p!
first_step: Write Σ_{C ≤ X} #{d | 4Cp+1, d ≡ −1 mod 4C} as Σ_d Σ_C 1[4Cp ≡ −1 mod d, d ≡ −1 mod 4C]; the d-sum with C free: for each d, the C with d ≡ −1 mod 4C ⟺ 4C | d+1. So count pairs (d, C) with 4C | d+1 and d | 4Cp+1 — rewrite and see if it reduces to a count of p in residue classes mod d (averaged over d) — Bombieri–Vinogradov at a single p? Check.
alt_first_steps: [signature-0388] Extract bounds for sum_{d|N, d≡−1 mod q}1 and specialize N to ES's p-tied forms.
refs: unverified: https://arxiv.org/search/?query=divisors+arithmetic+progressions+character+sums&searchtype=all

title: Reverse the roles: for each modulus m = 4C, list p for which some d|4Cp+1 is ≡ −1 mod m — a 'dual sieve' table
connection: Duality between p and modulus ↔ the set S_C = {p : C-slice succeeds} is a union of residue classes mod d for d ≡ −1 mod 4C.
why: S_C is periodic only if bounded d; with unbounded d it's a 'multiplicative' set. ES ⟺ ∪_C S_C ⊇ primes. Studying S_C's density and correlations between S_C, S_{C'} is a sieve-dimension question.
first_step: Compute densities of S_C among primes ≤ 10⁷ for C ≤ 30 and correlation matrix corr(1_{S_C}, 1_{S_{C'}}); test near-independence.

title: Trivially-forced divisibility at fixed p: 4Cp+1 ≡ 0 mod ℓ for C ≡ −(4p)^{-1} mod ℓ
connection: For each small prime ℓ, some C < ℓ gives ℓ | 4Cp+1 ↔ the divisor ℓ is in class −1 mod 4C only if ℓ ≡ −1 mod 4C — a 'self-levelled' small-prime certificate.
why: This is the cheapest structured certificate family (d = ℓ prime): ES(p) ⟸ ∃ ℓ prime, C | (ℓ+1)/4, ℓ | 4Cp+1. That's p ≡ −(4C)^{-1} mod ℓ — a residue condition mod ℓ for each divisor C of (ℓ+1)/4: density ≈ τ((ℓ+1)/4)/ℓ per ℓ, sum diverges like Σ τ/ℓ ~ log²: matches log² main term!
first_step: Compute the fraction of R(p) coming from d prime (vs composite) for p ≤ 10⁷; if prime d dominate, the problem is 'p in a union of residue classes mod primes ℓ' — classical sieve setting (B1/B2 still).

title: Ternary divisor problem: R(p) as τ₃-like count of factorisations 4uBC − u − B = p
connection: R(p) counts restricted 'three-factor' decompositions ↔ τ₃(n) has mean (log n)²/2 — matches R's log² scale!
why: Natural to compare R(p) with τ₃ of a p-tied integer (e.g. τ₃(4p+…)); maybe R(p) = Σ over a bounded set of τ₃(N_i(p)) restricted to classes.
first_step: Compute correlation between R(p) and τ₃(p+1), τ₃(p+3), τ(…) etc. for p ≤ 10⁶.

title: Exact formula: R(p) = Σ_{C} (τ_{−1 mod 4C}(4Cp+1)) — compute generating Dirichlet series in p
connection: Treat R(n) for all odd n: D(s) = Σ R(n) n^{-s} ↔ analytic properties (poles at s=1 of order 3?) give mean values; Tauberian.
why: Mean value ≍ log² — consistent with triple pole; a factorisation D(s) = ζ(s)^? L(s,…) would expose structure.
first_step: Compute D(s) formally: Σ_{u,B,C} (4uBC − u − B)^{-s}; find its analytic continuation properties numerically or via Mellin–Barnes.

title: Consecutive-integer rigidity on (p, p+Q]: can a block of integers avoid all divisors ≡ −1 mod 4(n−p)?
connection: Shift form asks whether every block p+1..p+Q contains n with a divisor ≡ −1 mod 4(n−p) ↔ Erdős–Selfridge/Sylvester–Schur-type theorems on prime factors of consecutive integers are pointwise.
why: The catch (recorded): each n needs a divisor in a class tied to its own offset, so CRT can make p+B avoid it for B ≤ Q (B1); but for B ~ √p the condition becomes 'n = p+B has a divisor ≡ −1 mod 4B in [4B−1, ...]', i.e. a factorisation near-square — Sylvester–Schur-type large-prime-factor results could interact.
first_step: Compute for hard p the distribution of contributing B (as fraction of √p); if many come from B ≍ √p, study whether 'consecutive integers near p have near-square factorisations with prescribed class' has literature (search 'divisors close to square root of consecutive integers').

title: Additive bases: is the set of 'certificate-friendly' integers an additive basis of finite order?
connection: Define A = {n : ES(n) has a certificate of a simple type}; additive basis results (Schnirelmann) ↔ multiplicative closure of ES (if ES(a) then ES(ka)).
why: ES set is multiplicatively closed upward (multiples); it's a 'multiplicative ideal-like' set — primitive elements are the problem. Primitive sets theory (Erdős primitive set conjecture proved by Lichtman) might apply to 'minimal ES-failures'.
first_step: Note: the set of n failing ES (if any) is closed under taking divisors >1? (If ES(d) then ES(n) for d|n, so failures' divisors fail.) So failures form a divisor-closed set ⊂ primes∪{1}-generated: only primes. Record the clean fact and think about primitive-set density bounds (Lichtman).

title: Erdős primitive set conjecture (Lichtman 2022) as structure for failures of related numerator problems
connection: For m/n problems with exceptions (m = 8), the minimal exceptions form a primitive set ↔ Σ 1/(n log n) ≤ that of primes (Lichtman).
why: For m ≥ 5 exceptions, primitive-set bounds constrain how exceptions are distributed; tells whether exceptions are 'prime-like'.
first_step: List minimal 8/n exceptions ≤ 10⁶ and compute Σ 1/(n log n); compare with primes' value.

title: Sieve of 'multiplicatively constrained' shifts: primes p with p+1, p+2, …, p+K all composed of primes in prescribed classes
connection: Simultaneous Landau–Ramanujan conditions on consecutive shifts p+B ↔ sieve of dimension Σ δ_B; such primes exist (heuristically) with density (log)^{−Σδ_B}.
why: Shows quantitatively how a (★)-failure is built: all small shifts must be 'class-constrained' integers. The 14 known failures could be checked against this mechanism.
first_step: For p = 409 and the other (★)-failures, factor p+B for B ≤ 50 and verify each is class-constrained mod 4B; identify the slowest-failing B.

title: Fermat's factorisation viewpoint: 4Cp+1 + Y² must be a square X² with X ≡ −1 (mod 2C)
connection: Fermat's method searches X ≥ √N with X² − N square ↔ ES certificate as a Fermat factorisation step landing in a class.
why: Near-square factorisations (d ≈ d') correspond to small Y; the class condition on X is a congruence on a 'quadratic progression' X² − N, amenable to quadratic-sieve-style analysis.
first_step: For hard p, run Fermat-style search on 4Cp+1 for X ≡ −1 mod 2C up to X ≤ √N + K and count hits vs prediction.

title: Quadratic sieve / CFRAC structure: smooth values of X² − 4Cp − 1 as a thick object at p
connection: QS finds many smooth X² − N (thick object of size ~ N^{1/2} smooth values per sieve interval) ↔ combine smooth relations to get a factorisation of N with prescribed class of factors?
why: Combining relations yields congruences of squares, i.e. a nontrivial factor gcd(X − Y, N) — whose class mod 4C is uncontrolled. But one can sieve over C as well (many N): a 2D thick object.
first_step: Prototype: for C ≤ 50 run a tiny QS on 4Cp+1 and record the classes mod 4C of the factors found; is −1 hit at least as often as random?

title: Parity-problem diagnosis: how strongly does slice success correlate with λ(4Cp+1)?
connection: Selberg's parity barrier: sieves cannot detect the parity of Ω ↔ slice C fails whenever 4Cp+1 is prime (λ = −1); if success is strongly parity-correlated, ES inherits the parity problem.
why: If ES-type events are parity-sensitive, sieve-only proofs are excluded for a structural reason (complementing B1/B2); if not, the obstruction lies elsewhere.
first_step: For p ≤ 10⁶ and C ≤ 50, compute P(slice succeeds | λ(4Cp+1) = ±1) and P(… | Ω = k).

title: Ford-style 'anatomy' model: which levels C can host a witness
connection: A random N with k = ω(N) prime factors has ≤ 2^k divisors; their residues mod 4C hit the class −1 with probability ≈ 1 − exp(−2^k/φ(4C)). With ω ≈ log log p, only levels C ≲ (log p)^{log 2} are 'likely' — an anatomy prediction for where ES witnesses live (cf. Ford's H(x,y,2y)).
why: Ford solved the divisor-in-interval problem via the anatomy of prime factors; the analogous divisor-in-class statistic would give a sharp prediction for the distribution of the smallest working level.
first_step: Compute, for hard primes p ≤ 10⁹, the smallest C with a (★) witness and compare its distribution with (log p)^{log 2}; regress on ω(4Cp+1).
refs: unverified: Ford 2008, The distribution of integers with a divisor in a given interval (Annals 168)

title: Equal-denominator / chain sub-problems (x | y | z) as solvable slices
connection: Restricting ES to chains x | y | z or to a fixed ratio y = kx gives two-variable divisor problems with explicit criteria; the diagonal x = y is empty for p ≡ 1 mod 4 (see diagonal item).
why: Each restricted slice is a 'line' in the sense of F34; knowing exactly which primes each slice covers sharpens the infinite-covering picture.
first_step: For k = 2..20 compute which hard primes ≤ 10⁷ admit solutions with y = kx; tabulate densities.

title: Primes p ≡ 1 mod 4 as norms: ES-hardness vs. splitting in many imaginary quadratic fields ℚ(√−uB)
connection: M_BM(p) small ⟺ χ_{−4uB}(p) = +1 for many small pairs, i.e. p splits in many ℚ(√−uB) — Chebotarev in a large compositum. Hard primes are 'maximally split' primes (F20, F29).
why: Gives an explicit adversarial family (primes totally split in the compositum of ℚ(i, √−ℓ) for ℓ ≤ L) and connects ES lower bounds to the least prime not totally split (Linnik/Lagarias–Odlyzko).
first_step: Compute R(p) for the first primes totally split in ℚ(i, √−3, √−5, √−7, √−11, …) (L up to 40) and compare with random p of same size.

title: Representation of p by x² + ny² for many n simultaneously (Cox) as a model of 'p a square mod everything small'
connection: Hard ES primes are squares modulo many small moduli (Mordell classes mod 840 are squares). Cox's theory characterises p = x² + ny² via ring class fields; the simultaneous version is a Chebotarev condition.
why: If ES-hardness is monotone in 'how many small forms represent p', one could try induction on a class-field tower.
first_step: For hard primes ≤ 10⁸ count n ≤ 100 with p = x² + ny² and correlate with R(p)/log²p.

title: Elliott–Halberstam-type level of distribution for divisor-in-class counts (Fouvry–Iwaniec, Friedlander–Iwaniec d₃)
connection: Distribution of τ-type functions in APs beyond √x is known for d₂ (Selberg/Hooley/Heath-Brown) and d₃ (Friedlander–Iwaniec, Fouvry–Kowalski–Michel). ES sums divisor-in-class counts over p-tied integers.
why: These give averages over moduli (B2); pointwise not. Still the best tools for the averaged ES problems (exceptional set).
first_step: Check whether the 3/4 exceptional-set barrier (F40) can be moved by a d₃-in-APs level beyond 1/2 input.

title: Bach–Sorenson explicit GRH least-prime bounds
connection: The least-prime-in-a-class problem has a single-input/single-witness formulation (F01,F21), and a finite exceptional regime controlled by explicit estimates. Its class-group characters resemble the character sums in ES (F20).
why: The explicit constants and effective character-sum machinery may help replace qualitative ES average results with a pointwise count bound.
first_step: Read Bach–Sorenson's explicit GRH bounds and identify the exact zero-sum inequality; test its analogue on the finite character expansion defining R(p).

title: Schinzel–Sierpiński on primes among shifted linear forms
connection: The existence of primes in structured shifted forms is a pointwise prime-witness problem (F01,F21), and it interacts with the conjectural prime-plus-one/prime-divisor structure of ES (F10,F33).
why: Sieve arguments for simultaneous shifted-prime conditions may be relevant to the prime-tied divisors 4Cp+1, even if the exact theorem is conditional.
first_step: Verify the exact Schinzel–Sierpiński statement intended by (p+1)/(q+1), then test its local admissibility conditions on ES's linear forms 4Cp+1.

title: Hooley's GRH result for x²+y²+z³
connection: A conditional pointwise representation by mixed-degree forms resembles ES's affine surface family and pointwise integral-witness problem (F01,F13,F21), with analytic prime-distribution input.
why: A hybrid quadratic/cubic representation is close enough geometrically to make its circle-method and L-function tools worth checking for ES's conic fibration.
first_step: Verify the exact Hooley theorem and hypotheses, then inspect its treatment of local factors and compare them with the ES surface's local densities.

title: Linnik dispersion applied to ES divisor counts
connection: Dispersion is designed to derive pointwise existence from averaged arithmetic progressions (F05,F21,F22), and ES's ★ count is itself a sum of progression-restricted divisor counts (F10,F20).
why: It is a concrete analytic bridge between known average estimates and a single-prime lower bound.
first_step: Form the bilinear sum over p and C from R(p), apply Cauchy-Schwarz/dispersion, and check whether off-diagonal terms are bounded by available divisor correlations.

title: Least prime in a progression and ES tied-divisor residues
connection: Arxiv:1309.3595 treats least primes in arithmetic progressions alongside least nonresidues, matching ES F10/F20/F29 and the residue-class existence question.
why: It gives verified conditional tools for small representatives in a residue class, potentially useful after ES is reduced to finding a suitable prime or divisor class.
first_step: Check whether any ES tied integer condition can be reformulated as a least-prime-in-progression condition without losing the same-parameter divisibility constraint.

title: Smooth-number equidistribution and ES divisor classes
connection: Soundararajan's theorem (arXiv:0707.0299) shows that y-smooth integers below x are equidistributed in reduced residue classes mod q for q < y^{4√e−ε}. This matches ES F10/F20/F21, while ES needs a pointwise tied divisor.
why: Restricting the tied integer to smooth values might permit stronger residue control and expose a dense subfamily of primes.
first_step: Read the modulus range in the theorem and test whether an ES family's tied integer can be forced smooth at a compatible modulus.

title: Prime-minus-one characterization of a bilinear-form complement
connection: OEIS A005097 identifies the complement of values represented by 2xy+x+y as n with 2n+1 prime. This shares F01/F02/F10/F16w: an exact prime-indexed criterion, a simple polynomial representation, and a complementary exceptional set.
why: An exact arithmetic characterization of representability through a linear transform of n is a useful model for turning ES witness existence into a primality/divisor condition.

title: Parity problem in sieve theory
connection: Sieve parity problems share F21, F22, F40 and explain why robust average estimates may fail to detect a single required arithmetic type.
why: Diagnosing a parity obstruction can direct effort toward extra structure rather than stronger sieve weights alone.
first_step: Check whether ES's restricted-divisor sequence has a parity-insensitive distribution indistinguishable from a counterexample sequence.

title: Linear sieve and switching principles
connection: Thin sequence sieve problems share F05, F22, F40 and often gain from switching between primal and dual variables.
why: A switching step could exploit the tied parameter/divisor feature rather than treat candidates as an arbitrary sequence.
first_step: Recast the ES divisor condition in both numerator and divisor variables and check whether a switching identity improves level of distribution.

title: Chebotarev and splitting-sensitive Diophantine families
connection: Splitting problems share F06, F29, F36; Chebotarev controls average prime classes but not necessarily a witness for every prime.
why: Separating the distribution-of-primes issue from the per-prime construction can focus the ES reduction.
first_step: List which ES identity families require p split in Q(i), and check whether a compositum's Frobenius classes encode them.

title: Residue-class divisor sums and real-character bias
connection: Divisor sums share F10, F20, F37; exceptional real characters can create one-sided fluctuations.
why: Understanding bias helps avoid a false expectation that generic cancellation forces every class to receive a divisor.
first_step: Compute the real-character contribution to the ES divisor count separately and see when it can dominate the error terms.

title: Maynard 'dense clusters of primes in subsets' for certificate families
connection: Maynard (Compositio 2016) shows any positive-density subset of admissible linear forms contains many simultaneously prime values; ES certificates are indexed by a dense set of linear forms in the C-parameter (4Cp+1, Cp+...).
why: Gives a combinatorial robustness: we need not control which certificate fires, only that a dense sub-family of forms is admissible at p.
first_step: Check whether the family {4Cp+1 : C ≤ X} with the divisor-in-class event can be recast as primality of auxiliary linear forms f = (4Cp+1)/d for d in a fixed finite set; test admissibility mod small primes.
refs: Maynard, Dense clusters of primes in subsets, Compositio Math. 152 (2016)

title: Zhang / Polymath8 smooth-moduli level of distribution with modulus 4C smooth
connection: Zhang and Polymath8a get primes equidistributed in APs to smooth moduli beyond x^{1/2}; in ES Type I the tied modulus 4C (or 4cd) is free to be chosen smooth.
why: Choosing C among smooth numbers gives well-factorable moduli, which is exactly where beyond-1/2 equidistribution (dispersion + Kloosterman) is available.
first_step: Restrict the ES Type I/II search to C that are y-smooth (y = log^2 p) and measure on data whether R(p) restricted to smooth C keeps the log^2 p main term (p ≤ 10^7).
refs: Zhang, Bounded gaps between primes, Ann. Math. 179 (2014)
Polymath, Variants of the Selberg sieve…, Res. Math. Sci. 1 (2014)

title: Lichtman beyond-square-root Goldbach/AP methods for tied moduli
connection: Lichtman (2023) improves level of distribution for primes in APs with well-factorable weights to x^{0.617…} and uses it for Goldbach-type counts; ES Type I/II counts are linear-sieve-like sums over moduli 4C.
why: Any improvement in the level for the ES counting function shrinks the exceptional set exponent (repo's E(N) ≪ N exp(−c(log N)^{3/4})).
first_step: Check whether Lichtman's well-factorable weights can be placed on the C-variable (4C | modulus) in the repo's exceptional-set argument (paper/es-threequarter-note.tex).
refs: Lichtman, Primes in arithmetic progressions to large moduli and Goldbach beyond the square-root barrier, arXiv:2309.08522

title: Fouvry–Radziwiłł level of distribution of unbalanced convolutions
connection: Fouvry–Radziwiłł show α*β with one short factor has level of distribution beyond 1/2 for all residue classes; ES divisor counts 1_{ab|N} are convolutions with one short divisor.
why: ES certificates typically use a small divisor a and a large cofactor — the unbalanced regime FR handle.
first_step: Express the Type II e-slice count as Σ_{a small} Σ_{b} 1_{ab = N} with class conditions and check whether FR's theorem (moduli to x^{1/2+δ}) applies when averaging over p in the exceptional-set argument.
refs: Fouvry–Radziwiłł, Level of distribution of unbalanced convolutions, arXiv:1811.08672

title: Guth–Maynard large values of Dirichlet polynomials → short-interval exceptional sets
connection: Guth–Maynard (2024) improve zero-density (Ingham 12/5 → 30/13) via large-values estimates; ES exceptional-set bounds pass through prime counts in short intervals/APs.
why: Zero-density improvements translate to shorter intervals where almost all ES-good primes are detected; could sharpen E(N) or the size of windows where every prime is covered.
first_step: Locate in the repo's exceptional-set notes which zero-density exponent is used and recompute the window exponent with A = 30/13.
refs: Guth–Maynard, New large value estimates for Dirichlet polynomials, arXiv:2405.20552

title: Matomäki–Radziwiłł at fixed p along the C-progression
connection: MR show bounded multiplicative functions have the same mean in almost all short intervals as in long ones; the integers 4Cp+1 (C varying) form an AP of modulus 4p at fixed p.
why: A short-AP version (Klurman–Mangerel–Teräväinen) could show divisor-class statistics of 4Cp+1 in short C-windows match long averages for one fixed p — pointwise in p, average over C.
first_step: Check whether Klurman–Mangerel–Teräväinen 'multiplicative functions in short arithmetic progressions' covers modulus q = 4p with interval length X = p^{θ}; compute what θ the ES Type I count needs.
refs: Matomäki–Radziwiłł, Multiplicative functions in short intervals, Ann. Math. 183 (2016), arXiv:1501.04585

title: Linear correlations of restricted divisor functions (Matthiesen-type) with p as a coefficient
connection: Matthiesen proved asymptotics for Σ_t Π_i f(L_i(t)) for divisor-type f via the Green–Tao machinery. R(p) is Σ_C of a restricted divisor function of the linear form 4pC + 1; with more structure (several levels) it becomes a correlation.
why: Gives asymptotics with uniformity questions in the coefficient p — the precise point to check.
first_step: Matthiesen, 'Linear correlations of multiplicative functions', Proc. LMS 121 (2020), arXiv:1606.04482 — verified: fixed linear forms only, coefficients may NOT grow with the range; so the needed input is a uniform-in-coefficients version — state it precisely and look for partial results (e.g. for τ-type functions via Kloosterman methods).
alt_first_steps: [tools-0013] Check whether 'number of divisors ≡ −1 mod q' restricted divisor functions satisfy Matthiesen's hypotheses (they are not multiplicative but are sums over characters mod q of multiplicative functions).
refs: arXiv:math/0404188 (Green-Tao, primes contain arbitrarily long APs)
Matthiesen, Linear correlations of multiplicative functions, arXiv:1606.04482

title: de la Bretèche–Drappeau level of distribution of quadratic polynomials
connection: de la Bretèche–Drappeau (JEMS 2020) prove level of distribution beyond 1 for #{n ≤ x : q | n² + D} averaged over q; ES Type I is 'f | p² + 4c²d with f ≡ −p (mod 4cd)'.
why: Exactly the object (divisors of a quadratic value) with level > 1 — needed when f is larger than the square root.
first_step: Check whether their result allows a residue condition f ≡ a (mod 4cd) on the modulus f itself, and whether the polynomial variable can be c (with p fixed).
refs: de la Bretèche–Drappeau, Niveau de répartition des polynômes quadratiques et crible majorant pour les entiers friables, JEMS 22 (2020)

title: Duke–Friedlander–Iwaniec / Tóth equidistribution of roots of quadratic congruences with modulus condition
connection: Roots ν/f of ν² ≡ −D (mod f) equidistribute (DFI 1995 primes, Tóth composite); ES Type I asks that p be such a root (p² ≡ −4c²d mod f) while f ≡ −p mod 4cd — a joint condition on root and modulus.
why: Joint equidistribution of (root mod f, f mod m) pairs is a natural theorem to aim for and would give averaged Type I counts in new ranges.
first_step: Compute empirically, for D = 4c²d fixed small and f ≤ 10^6, the joint distribution of (ν/f, f mod 4cd) and check for correlation.
refs: Duke–Friedlander–Iwaniec, Equidistribution of roots of a quadratic congruence to prime moduli, Ann. Math. 141 (1995)

title: Fouvry–Kowalski–Michel trace functions over primes for ES residue indicators
connection: FKM show algebraic trace functions K(n) mod q have Σ_{p≤x} K(p) = o(π(x)) for x ≥ q^{3/4+ε}; ES conditions like '(−p mod 4C) ∈ some set' are trace-function-type functions of p.
why: Gives equidistribution of primes p against arbitrary algebraic weights — e.g. the set of p for which a given finite menu fails mod q.
first_step: Check whether the 'menu failure' indicator mod a prime q (FIXED_MODULUS_SHOTS.md) is a bounded-conductor trace function and apply FKM to get prime densities.
refs: Fouvry–Kowalski–Michel, Algebraic trace functions over the primes, Duke Math. J. 163 (2014)

title: Irving / Liu–Shparlinski–Zhang divisor function in APs to smooth or prime-power moduli
connection: Irving (2015) and Liu–Shparlinski–Zhang get τ(n) equidistributed in APs to smooth / prime-power moduli beyond 2/3; ES's tied modulus 4C can be chosen a power of 2 times smooth.
why: Choosing 4C = 2^k is a legitimate ES sub-family (TWO_POWER_LADDER) and prime-power moduli have extra equidistribution.
first_step: Compare TWO_POWER_LADDER.md counts with the divisor-in-AP-to-2^k asymptotic; check which range of k the LSZ theorem covers.
refs: Irving, The divisor function in arithmetic progressions to smooth moduli, IMRN 2015
Liu–Shparlinski–Zhang, Divisor problem in arithmetic progressions modulo a prime power, Adv. Math. (2018)

title: Granville–Koukoulopoulos–Matomäki 'when the sieve works'
connection: GKM (Duke 2015) characterise when sifted sets by a set of primes have the expected density; the 'divisors avoid a coset structure' condition in ES is a sifted-set condition on prime factors of 4Cp+1.
why: Precise conditions for sieve heuristics to be correct are what a pointwise lower-tail claim needs.
first_step: Check whether the sifting set 'primes ℓ whose class mod 4C lies in a subgroup H not containing −1' satisfies GKM hypotheses uniformly in C.
refs: Granville–Koukoulopoulos–Matomäki, When the sieve works, Duke Math. J. 164 (2015)

title: Ford–Maynard theory of prime-producing sieves
connection: Ford–Maynard analyse which sieve-theoretic information (Type I/II ranges) can and cannot produce primes, extending the parity problem; ES is a 'one witness among polylog' problem with a parity-like barrier.
why: A formal limit theory for sieve information could make the campaign's B-barriers precise or show a gap.
first_step: Check whether Ford–Maynard's framework (arXiv 2024) includes sequences where the target is 'has a divisor in a class' rather than 'is prime'.
refs: Ford–Maynard, On the theory of prime producing sieves, arXiv:2407.14368

title: Erdős primitive-set / Lichtman: ES-covered n as a set of multiples
connection: Since a solution for n gives one for every multiple of n, the set of n covered by any fixed family of identities is a set of multiples ℳ(B) of a primitive set B; Lichtman (2022) proved the Erdős primitive set conjecture Σ 1/(b log b) ≤ Σ_p 1/(p log p).
why: Sets-of-multiples theory (Besicovitch, Erdős, Hall) quantifies how much a family covers and how the uncovered set (divisor-closed) can look.
first_step: For the repo's identity menus up to modulus M, compute the primitive generator set B among primes ≤ 10^7 and the density of ℳ(B); test whether Σ_{b∈B} 1/(b log b) tracks the uncovered density.
refs: Lichtman, A proof of the Erdős primitive set conjecture, arXiv:2202.02384
Hall, Sets of Multiples (CUP 1996)

title: Harel–Mousset–Samotij upper tails via entropic stability (dual for R(p))
connection: HMS 'Upper tails via high moments and entropic stability' gives sharp upper tails for subgraph counts; for ES, upper-tail control of the *failure* indicator counts translates into exceptional-set bounds.
why: Exceptional-set results are upper tails of a 'number of uncovered p' variable.
first_step: Write E(N) as a polynomial count and check whether HMS-type moment methods give anything beyond Vaughan-type bounds.
refs: Harel–Mousset–Samotij, Upper tails via high moments and entropic stability, Duke Math. J. (2022), arXiv:1904.08212

title: Granville–Soundararajan pretentiousness of the 'class of divisors' character
connection: Pretentious theory: a multiplicative function f is small on average unless it pretends to be n^{it}χ(n); the indicator of 'N has a divisor in class −1 mod m' expands via characters χ mod m into Σ_χ χ̄(−1) Σ_{d|N} χ(d).
why: The ES failure set is where all such character divisor sums conspire; pretentious distance gives a language for 'conspiracy'.
first_step: For each failing N (no divisor ≡ −1 mod m), compute the pretentious distance D(χ_m-twisted divisor sums) and see whether failures cluster at a pretentious character (e.g. the real character mod m).
refs: Granville–Soundararajan, Large character sums: pretentious characters and the Pólya–Vinogradov theorem, JAMS 20 (2007)

title: Ustinov's Kloosterman-sum method for continued-fraction length statistics
connection: Ustinov computes asymptotics of the number of a/b with prescribed CF statistics by reducing to lattice-point counts with Kloosterman sums; ES₅ is λ(p) ≤ 3 (a length-3 CF event).
why: Gives exact averaged main terms with power savings for CF-length events, possibly pointwise-in-p with a C-average.
first_step: Reproduce Ustinov's count of (a,b) with a/b having CF length 3 and specialize to b tied to p.
refs: Ustinov, papers on the distribution of continued fraction statistics (Sb. Math. 2005–2013)

title: Pierce–Turnage-Butterbaugh–Wood effective Chebotarev in families → small split primes
connection: PTW (Invent. 2020) prove effective Chebotarev for almost all fields in families, giving ℓ-torsion bounds; ES certificates need small primes split in Q(√−d)-type fields tied to p.
why: Families of fields indexed by d or C at fixed p are exactly where 'almost all fields' results bite.
first_step: Identify the field family {Q(√−d), ray class fields mod 4cd} relevant to Type I and check whether PTW's family hypotheses hold.
refs: Pierce–Turnage-Butterbaugh–Wood, An effective Chebotarev density theorem for families of number fields, with an application to ℓ-torsion in class groups, Invent. Math. 219 (2020), arXiv:1709.09637

title: Y. Zhang's Landau–Siegel preprint (claimed) as alternate effectivity input
connection: Yitang Zhang's 2022 preprint claims L(1,χ) ≫ (log D)^{−2022}; same effectivity consequences as above.
why: A second independent route to effective Siegel-type input.
first_step: Check the current status (errata, refereeing) of Zhang's arXiv:2211.02515 before relying on it.

title: Drappeau–Pratt–Radziwiłł one-level density beyond (−2,2) via Kloosterman sums
connection: DPR extend one-level density support for Dirichlet L-functions using sums of Kloosterman sums (Deshouillers–Iwaniec spectral input); ES counts reduce to sums over characters mod 4C at fixed p.
why: Shows a pathway where spectral Kloosterman bounds give information about families of characters — the ES character expansion is such a family.
first_step: Check whether the ES Type I count summed over C ≤ X is a 'family of characters' average where DPR-style spectral input applies.
refs: Drappeau–Pratt–Radziwiłł, One-level density estimates for Dirichlet L-functions with extended support, arXiv:2002.11968

title: Pascadi exceptional Maass form large sieve → ES dispersion
connection: Pascadi (2024) proves large sieve inequalities for exceptional Maass forms improving dispersion estimates (primes in APs to large moduli); the repo's exceptional-set argument uses dispersion-type steps.
why: Better exceptional-eigenvalue control improves level of distribution in the Type II dispersion step.

refs: Pascadi, Large sieve inequalities for exceptional Maass forms and applications, arXiv:2404.04239

title: Bourgain–Glibichuk–Konyagin exponential sums over small multiplicative subgroups
connection: BGK: subgroups H ⊂ 𝔽_p^× with |H| > p^δ have nontrivial exponential sums; the subgroup generated by small primes / prime factors of N mod e is such an H.
why: Additive equidistribution of H mod e could feed into counts of e with −1 ∈ ⟨factors of N⟩.
first_step: For e prime, compute |⟨prime factors of (p+e)/4⟩| in 𝔽_e^× at hard primes and check how often −1 ∈ H fails (equivalently |H| odd).
refs: Bourgain–Glibichuk–Konyagin, Estimates for the number of sums and products and for exponential sums in fields of prime order, J. LMS 73 (2006)

title: Sum-product in ℤ/q for composite q (Bourgain) for ES moduli 4C
connection: Bourgain's sum-product and exponential-sum bounds for arbitrary q handle composite moduli; ES moduli 4C, 4cd are composite and smooth.
why: The ES condition mixes additive (4Cp+1) and multiplicative (divisor class) structure — a sum-product configuration.
first_step: State the ES Type I condition as 'A + B ∩ product set' in ℤ/4C and check whether Bourgain's composite-modulus results say anything at C ≈ p^θ.
refs: Bourgain, Exponential sum estimates over subgroups of Z_q^*, q arbitrary, J. Anal. Math. 97 (2005)

title: Absorption method (Keevash / Kwan–Sah–Sawhney–Simkin) — 'almost all → all' gadgets
connection: Iterative absorption converts near-perfect structures into perfect ones by pre-reserving absorbers; ES knows almost-all results, and the missing step is exactly almost-all → all.
why: If ES solutions for n could be built from solutions of auxiliary numbers with an 'absorber' reserving flexibility, the exceptional set could be absorbed.
first_step: Look for an ES operation combining solutions of several auxiliary integers (m1,…,mk tied to p) into a solution for p; test on data whether such auxiliary sets always contain a solvable member.
refs: Keevash, The existence of designs, arXiv:1401.3665
Kwan–Sah–Sawhney–Simkin, High-girth Steiner triple systems, arXiv:2201.04554

title: Szemerédi regularity / arithmetic regularity (Green; Green–Tao) for the failure set
connection: Arithmetic regularity decomposes any set into structured + pseudorandom parts; the ES failure set E is divisor-closed and scales from q ≡ 3 (mod 4) can't fill an AP.
why: Arithmetic regularity applied to E (if nonempty, hypothetically) would force structure contradicting known closure properties — a disproof-shape calibration.
first_step: List all closure properties E must satisfy (divisor-closed, avoids identity classes, density zero) and check whether arithmetic regularity yields a contradiction for positive relative density in primes.
refs: Green–Tao, An arithmetic regularity lemma, an associated counting lemma, and applications, arXiv:1002.2028

title: Green–Tao relative Szemerédi / dense model for ES-good primes
connection: Green–Tao transference finds structure in dense subsets of primes; the set of ES-hard primes (not covered by identities of modulus ≤ M) is a structured subset of primes.
why: Could prove infinitely many patterns (APs) among primes p whose ES solutions have a specific shape — an existence-of-structure statement.
first_step: Check whether 'primes with an ES Type I certificate with C ≤ K' has positive relative density in primes; if so Green–Tao yields APs of them.
refs: Green–Tao, The primes contain arbitrarily long arithmetic progressions, Ann. Math. 167 (2008)
Conlon–Fox–Zhao, A relative Szemerédi theorem, GAFA 25 (2015)

title: Green–Tao–Ziegler linear equations in primes for prime-denominator ES solutions
connection: GTZ count prime solutions of finite-complexity linear systems; ES solutions with prime denominators reduce to linear equations after fixing products (e.g. Type II with x = (p+e)/4 prime-parametrised).
why: Counting prime-denominator ES solutions across p gives averaged statements with primes in all slots.
first_step: Enumerate ES solution shapes where all three denominators are of the form (linear form in parameters) and identify a finite-complexity linear system in primes.
refs: Green–Tao, Linear equations in primes, Ann. Math. 171 (2010)

title: Peluse–Prendiville polynomial Szemerédi with power saving
connection: Peluse–Prendiville give power-saving bounds for sets avoiding x, x+y, x+y² etc.; ES identities often involve quadratic expressions in the parameter (Mordell families).
why: Degree-lowering for polynomial configurations could detect quadratic ES families within dense sets of n.
first_step: List Mordell-family identities as polynomial configurations (n, n+P1(t), …) and check whether they are of PP type.
refs: Peluse, Bounds for sets with no polynomial progressions, Forum Math. Pi 8 (2020), arXiv:1909.00309

title: Erdős–Szemerédi sum-product / Solymosi for ES additive-multiplicative mixing
connection: Sum-product phenomenon: A+A or A·A large; the ES integer families {4Cp+1} are additive shifts while certificates are multiplicative.
why: Sum-product heuristics predict that additive families can't stay multiplicatively structured, supporting divisor-class equidistribution.
first_step: Measure multiplicative energy of {4Cp+1 : C ≤ X} vs random integers of the same size.
refs: Solymosi, Bounding multiplicative energy by the sumset, Adv. Math. 222 (2009)

title: Decoupling/energy for the hyperbolic ES surface {4uBC − u − B}
connection: BDG decoupling bounds moments of exponential sums over curves. Additive energy of the ES-word set (#{w₁ = w₂} with w = 4uBC−u−B ≤ N) controls the second moment Σ_n R(n)².
why: Second-moment control is the ingredient of every almost-all → pointwise attempt via variance; decoupling-type bounds for this specific surface could be sharp.
first_step: Compute the energy E(N) = Σ_{n≤N} R(n)² for N up to 10⁷ and fit N·(log N)^a; compare with what a decoupling inequality for (u, B, uB) would predict.
alt_first_steps: [tools-0105] Write Σ_n f(n) e(nα) as an exponential sum over the surface and identify a moment-curve-like structure for decoupling.
refs: arXiv:1512.01565 (Bourgain-Demeter-Guth)
Bourgain–Demeter–Guth, Proof of the main conjecture in Vinogradov's mean value theorem for degrees higher than three, Ann. Math. 184 (2016), arXiv:1512.01565

title: Wooley efficient congruencing / nested efficient congruencing for ES moments
connection: Efficient congruencing gives sharp mean values via p-adic concentration iteration; ES solution counts mod prime powers have a p-adic concentration structure (Hensel lifts of certificates).
why: Moment bounds Σ f(n)^k with sharp exponents constrain the distribution of R(p).
first_step: Compute numerically Σ_{n ≤ N} f(n)^2, f(n)^3 and fit exponents of log N; compare with decoupling-type predictions.
refs: Wooley, Nested efficient congruencing and relatives of Vinogradov's mean value theorem, Proc. LMS 118 (2019)

title: Pila–Wilkie / Binyamini–Novikov sharply o-minimal counting for ES real-analytic families
connection: Pila–Wilkie counts rational points on transcendental parts of definable sets; Binyamini–Novikov(–Zack) give effective polylog versions for sharply o-minimal structures. ES counting functions involve log-like main terms in a definable family (the real points of U_n as n varies).
why: The count M_BM(p) ≍ log² p is polylogarithmic — the same scale as sharply o-minimal point counts; a structural explanation of 'polylog' could come from there.
first_step: Check whether the set {(n, x/n, y/n, z/n)} is definable in ℝ_exp after a log-scaling and whether its algebraic part is all of it (then Pila–Wilkie says nothing).
